chapter: Benny Carter, saxophones and Coleman Hawkins's last years
title: How teaching changed Benny Carter and Cozy Cole's playing
summary: Dance and Caldwell feel that musicians who teach for years lose some of their edge.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Have you heard him play in recent years?
I heard him play on that Channel 13 when they was honoring --
Yeah. You know, it's a funny thing to me, the way -- now, he -- he sort of did change his style quite a bit after Charlie Parker.

Yeah, because -- well, in fact what I think it is, Stanley, because I listened to him too because I can notice the difference, you know, being knowing him through the years and worked with him when we were coming along around New York, and mostly he been teaching. And he always do -- every year he goes to Princeton University. He holds a class over there. And he always -- if he come to

New York, he's always on the Newport jazz thing or the (unintelligible) recorder, and sometimes I imagine when he start to do more like teaching and all, it kind of takes a slide (unintelligible) a little bit different, you know, than it would if you just keep actually playing. I think that's what it was because I could tell the difference too.
Well, you -- you know, it always seemed to me that in a different way that was the same with Cozy Cole. I mean Cozy, you used to hear him on records. He was rather an exciting drummer guy.
But after he had those years teaching, well, that's a different thing.
It takes something away from them.
It's okay, but it's so stiff, you know?
